content: Real estate investment trusts (“REITs”) have been around for more than fifty years. Congress established REITs in 1960 to allow individual investors to invest in large-scale, income-producing real estate. REITs provide a way for individual investors to earn a share of the income produced through commercial real estate ownership – without actually having to go out and buy commercial real estate.
section_heading: Investor Bulletin: Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs)

content: A REIT, generally, is a company that owns – and typically operates – income-producing real estate or real estate-related assets. The income-producing real estate assets owned by a REIT may include office buildings, shopping malls, apartments, hotels, resorts, self-storage facilities, warehouses, and mortgages or loans. Most REITs specialize in a single type of real estate – for example, apartment communities. There are retail REITs, office REITs, residential REITs, healthcare REITs, and industrial REITs, to name a few. What distinguishes REITs from other real estate companies is that a REIT must acquire and develop its real estate properties primarily to operate them as part of its own investment portfolio, as opposed to reselling those properties after they have been developed.

To qualify as a REIT, a company must have the bulk of its assets and income connected to real estate investment and must distribute at least 90 percent of its taxable income to shareholders annually in the form of dividends. A company that qualifies as a REIT is allowed to deduct from its corporate taxable income all of the dividends that it pays out to its shareholders. Because of this special tax treatment, most REITs pay out at least 100 percent of their taxable income to their shareholders and, therefore, owe no corporate tax.
section_heading: How to Qualify as a REIT?

content: In addition to paying out at least 90 percent of its taxable income annually in the form of shareholder dividends, a REIT must: be an entity that would be taxable as a corporation but for its REIT status; be managed by a board of directors or trustees; have shares that are fully transferable; have a minimum of 100 shareholders after its first year as a REIT; have no more than 50 percent of its shares held by five or fewer individuals during the last half of the taxable year; invest at least 75 percent of its total assets in real estate assets and cash; derive at least 75 percent of its gross income from real estate related sources, including rents from real property and interest on mortgages financing real property; derive at least 95 percent of its gross income from such real estate sources and dividends or interest from any source; and have no more than 25 percent of its assets consist of non-qualifying securities or stock in taxable REIT subsidiaries.
section_heading: How to Qualify as a REIT? — Requirements

content: REITs generally fall into three categories: equity REITs, mortgage REITs, and hybrid REITs. Most REITs are equity REITs. Equity REITs typically own and operate income-producing real estate. Mortgage REITs provide money to real estate owners and operators either directly in the form of mortgages or other types of real estate loans, or indirectly through the acquisition of mortgage-backed securities. Mortgage REITs tend to be more leveraged (that is, they use a lot of borrowed capital) than equity REITs. Many mortgage REITs manage their interest rate and credit risks through derivatives and other hedging techniques. Investors should understand the risks of these strategies before deciding to invest in these types of REITs. Hybrid REITs generally use the investment strategies of both equity REITs and mortgage REITs.
section_heading: Three Categories of REITs: Equity, Mortgage, and Hybrid

content: Because they often invest in debt securities secured by residential and commercial mortgages, mortgage REITs can be similar to certain investment companies that are focused on real estate. Generally, companies that invest a majority of their assets in real estate are exempted from the rules that govern investment companies, such as mutual funds. The SEC has initiated a review to determine whether certain mortgage REITs should continue to be exempt from investment company regulation. Those rules generally limit the amount of leverage that a fund can use and regulate the fees that can be charged to investors.
section_heading: Mortgage REITs and Investment Company Regulation

content: Many REITs (whether equity or mortgage) are registered with the SEC and are publicly traded on a stock exchange. These are known as publicly traded REITs. In addition, there are REITs that are registered with the SEC, but are not publicly traded. These are known as non-traded REITs (also known as non-exchange traded REITs). The bulletin compares the characteristics of publicly traded and non-traded REITs.
section_heading: Comparison of Publicly Traded REITs and Non-Traded REITs

content: Overview: Publicly traded REITs file reports with the SEC and their shares trade on national stock exchanges. Non-traded REITs file reports with the SEC but their shares do not trade on national stock exchanges. Liquidity: Publicly traded REIT shares are listed and traded like any publicly traded stock on major stock exchanges; most are NYSE listed. Non-traded REIT shares are not traded on public stock exchanges. Redemption programs vary by company and are typically very limited. Investors may have to wait for return of capital until the company lists shares on an exchange or liquidates its assets.
section_heading: Comparison of Publicly Traded REITs and Non-Traded REITs — Overview and Liquidity

content: Transaction costs: Brokerage costs for publicly traded REITs are the same as for buying or selling any other publicly traded stock. For non-traded REITs, fees of 9–10 percent of the investment are typically charged for broker-dealer commissions and other upfront offering costs. Ongoing acquisition and management fees and other expenses are also typical, and back-end fees may be charged.
section_heading: Comparison of Publicly Traded REITs and Non-Traded REITs — Transaction Costs

content: Management: Publicly traded REIT managers are typically employees of the company. Non-traded REITs typically have no employees and are managed by a third party under a management contract. Minimum investment amount: one share for publicly traded REITs; typically $1,000–$2,500 for non-traded REITs. Independent directors: stock exchange rules require a majority of publicly traded REIT directors to be independent of management; NYSE and NASDAQ rules call for fully independent audit, nominating, and compensation committees. NASAA guidelines adopted by many states require a majority of non-traded REIT directors to be independent and a majority of each board committee to consist of independent directors. Investor control: investors elect directors in both categories. Corporate governance: publicly traded REITs are subject to specific stock exchange rules; non-traded REITs are subject to state and NASAA guidelines. Disclosure: both must make regular SEC disclosures, including quarterly financial reports and yearly audited financial reports.
section_heading: Comparison of Publicly Traded REITs and Non-Traded REITs — Management, Investment, Governance, and Disclosure

content: Share value transparency: Real-time market prices for publicly traded REITs are publicly available, and a wide range of analyst reports is available. For non-traded REITs, no independent information about share value is available; the company may provide an estimated share value 18 months after the offering has closed. Source noted in the bulletin: National Association of Real Estate Investment Trusts (NAREIT).
section_heading: Comparison of Publicly Traded REITs and Non-Traded REITs — Share Value Transparency

content: Lack of liquidity: Non-traded REITs are illiquid investments and generally cannot be sold readily on the open market. If an investor needs to sell an asset quickly to raise money, shares of a non-traded REIT may not be saleable. Redemption programs are typically subject to significant limitations and may be discontinued at the company's discretion. Investors may have to wait for return of capital until a listing or liquidation; such events may occur more than 10 years after the investment. Share value transparency: Unlike publicly traded REITs, non-traded REITs have no exchange market price. They typically do not provide an estimate of value per share until 18 months after their offering closes, which may be years after investment. Investors may be unable to assess the investment's value or volatility for a significant period.
section_heading: Some Caveats about Non-Traded REITs — Lack of Liquidity and Share Value Transparency

content: Significant up-front fees: Non-traded REITs are typically sold by financial advisers and generally have high upfront fees that reduce the value of the investment. Sales commissions and upfront offering fees are usually approximately 9–10 percent; a portion of the share purchase price represents commissions, reducing the amount actually invested in the company. Distributions may be paid from offering proceeds and borrowings: Investors should consider total return (capital appreciation plus dividends), not only dividend yield. Non-traded REITs frequently pay distributions in excess of funds from operations, using offering proceeds and borrowings; this can reduce share value and cash available to purchase additional assets. Investors should assess the extent to which distributions come from sources other than funds from operations. Conflicts of interest: Non-traded REITs are typically externally managed and may pay significant fees to managers for activities such as property acquisitions and assets under management. These fees may not align with shareholder interests, and the external manager may manage competing companies.
section_heading: Some Caveats about Non-Traded REITs — Fees, Distributions, and Conflicts of Interest

content: As with any investment, investors should take their own financial situation into account, consult a financial adviser, and perform thorough research before making investment decisions concerning REITs. REIT disclosure filings, including annual and quarterly reports and offering prospectuses, can be reviewed at sec.gov. Investors can buy publicly traded REIT shares through a broker, as with other publicly traded securities. Generally, they can purchase common stock, preferred stock, or debt securities of a publicly traded REIT. Shares of a non-traded REIT can be purchased through a broker engaged in its offering. Investors can also purchase shares in a REIT mutual fund (index or actively managed) or a REIT exchange-traded fund.

REIT shareholders are responsible for paying taxes on dividends they receive and on capital gains associated with their investment. REIT dividends generally are treated as ordinary income and are not entitled to the reduced tax rates available for other types of corporate dividends. For this reason, some investors prefer to hold REIT shares or REIT funds in a tax-deferred account, such as a retirement account, to defer taxes on dividends and capital gains until they withdraw money from the account. A REIT is not a pass-through entity; unlike a partnership, it cannot pass tax losses through to investors. The bulletin recommends consulting a tax adviser before investing in REITs.
